children.text: Historical Simulation replays actual history. Parametric VaR assumes a shape and solves it with a formula. Monte Carlo simulation sits between the two: you choose a model for how returns behave, then generate thousands of computer-simulated futures from it, and treat the result exactly like a Historical Simulation, sort the outcomes, read off the percentile. The difference is that the scenarios are manufactured, not observed, which is both its biggest strength and the thing you have to be most careful about.

body.label: Monte Carlo VaR
body.value: Simulate thousands of possible future paths from a chosen model, fully revalue the portfolio on each, sort the outcomes, and read off the percentile
body.context: Unlike Historical Simulation, you are not limited to scenarios that actually happened.

children.text: Step by Step: Building a Monte Carlo VaR

One, choose a stochastic model and a distribution for the underlying risk factor, for a stock or index this is usually Geometric Brownian Motion driven by a normal or fatter-tailed distribution. Two, draw thousands of random outcomes from that distribution, typically 10,000 to 100,000 for a single-asset book, and generate a simulated terminal value for each. Three, fully revalue the portfolio under every single simulated outcome, this is the step that gives Monte Carlo its edge, covered below. Four, sort every simulated profit or loss and pick the percentile, exactly like Historical Simulation.

body.caption: Geometric Brownian Motion for simulating a terminal price. Z is a random draw. This is built directly on the log returns from Chapter 1, which is exactly why log returns rather than simple returns are the standard choice for simulation.

body.text: At a 1-day horizon, the drift term and the minus-half-sigma-squared correction are both tiny next to the volatility term, so the formula collapses close to S_T = S_0 x exp(sigma x Z), using the exact same daily volatility estimate from Chapter 1. Over a multi-day horizon those smaller terms stop being negligible, which is one reason Monte Carlo is often preferred over the square-root-of-time shortcut for longer-horizon VaR.

children.text: Worked Example: Normal Draws vs Fat-Tailed Draws

cells: Rs 50,00,000 tracking Nifty (same as the Chapter 2 Parametric example)
Student-t draws, 5 degrees of freedom, variance-matched to the same 1.2% volatility

body.text: The normal-draw Monte Carlo result and the closed-form Parametric result land close to each other, Rs 1,33,799 versus Rs 1,39,560 at 99% confidence. That is exactly what should happen: when Monte Carlo uses the same normal distribution assumption as the Parametric method, it should converge toward the same answer. The small gap is simulation error, not a modeling disagreement, and it shrinks as you increase the number of paths. This convergence check is a standard sanity test before trusting a Monte Carlo model on a live book.

stats.label: Student-t MC, 95% VaR
stats.context: Same run, fatter-tailed draws, 5 degrees of freedom

body.text: Look carefully at both confidence levels together. At 95%, the Student-t VaR is actually slightly lower than the normal VaR, Rs 92,629 versus Rs 95,397. At 99%, it is 17% higher. This is not a mistake, fat tails do not raise VaR uniformly across every confidence level, they concentrate extra probability mass deep in the tail while pulling slightly more mass toward the center, so a t-distribution with the same overall volatility can look milder at 95% and noticeably more severe at 99% or 99.9%. This is exactly why Chapter 3's discussion of Expected Shortfall matters: a VaR comparison at a single confidence level can miss how differently two models behave in the extreme tail.

body.code:
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)
S0, sigma, V, n_paths = 24000, 0.012, 5_000_000, 20_000

Z = np.random.standard_normal(n_paths)
returns = (-0.5 * sigma**2) + sigma * Z
pnl = (np.exp(returns) - 1) * V

sorted_pnl = np.sort(pnl)
var_95 = -sorted_pnl[int(0.05 * n_paths)]
var_99 = -sorted_pnl[int(0.01 * n_paths)]

print(f"95% 1-day Monte Carlo VaR: Rs {var_95:,.0f}")
print(f"99% 1-day Monte Carlo VaR: Rs {var_99:,.0f}")
body.caption: The core Monte Carlo VaR routine. Running this exact code will not reproduce the precise rupee figures quoted above, they came from a separate run, which is itself the point: note the seed, and expect small run-to-run differences unless you fix it. Swap np.random.standard_normal for a Student-t or bootstrap-from-history sampler and everything downstream, sorting, percentile lookup, stays identical.

children.text: Where Monte Carlo Earns Its Keep: Full Revaluation for Options

The last lesson flagged delta-normal Parametric VaR's weak spot: it approximates an option's curved, convex payoff with a straight line, which understates risk on large moves. Monte Carlo does not need that approximation. At each of the 20,000 simulated terminal prices, you fully reprice the option, using Black-Scholes or a more exact model, rather than extrapolating along a straight delta line. The simulated P&L distribution then automatically reflects the option's true convexity, gamma risk included, without any separate correction.

body.title: Delta-Normal Parametric vs Monte Carlo Full Revaluation, for an Options Book

columns.label: Delta-Normal Parametric
points: Approximates the option payoff with a straight line at current delta
Fast, closed-form
Captures directional risk reasonably, misses gamma risk
Can understate risk badly for short-gamma positions in a large move

columns.label: Monte Carlo Full Revaluation
points: Reprices the actual option payoff at every simulated terminal price
Computationally heavier, especially for large multi-option books
Captures gamma risk and convexity correctly by construction
Standard choice for complex derivatives desks and path-dependent instruments

body.title: Monte Carlo VaR: Strengths and Weaknesses

columns.label: Strengths
points: You can plug in any distribution, normal, Student-t, or a bootstrap from real historical returns
Handles nonlinear, path-dependent, and multi-leg option positions correctly through full revaluation
Can model multiple correlated risk factors jointly, not just a single asset
Not limited to scenarios that have actually occurred in history

columns.label: Weaknesses
points: Computationally expensive, especially with full revaluation across a large derivatives book
Still built on a chosen model and distribution, garbage assumptions in, garbage VaR out
Results carry simulation error and depend on the number of paths run
Correlation and volatility inputs face the same estimation challenges as the Parametric method

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A risk team runs a Monte Carlo VaR twice with the same model and inputs, once with 1,000 paths and once with 100,000 paths. The two runs give slightly different VaR figures. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The underlying position changed between the two runs
Simulation error: with fewer paths, the percentile estimate is noisier and varies more from run to run
The 1,000-path run used a different confidence level
Monte Carlo VaR is only valid with exactly 10,000 paths
body.explanation: Monte Carlo estimates converge toward a stable answer as the number of simulated paths grows, but any finite number of paths carries sampling noise. A 1,000-path run has noticeably more of this simulation error than a 100,000-path run, which is why desks check for convergence before trusting a Monte Carlo VaR figure.

body.title: Choosing a Method for an Options Book
body.scenario: A desk manages a book of short Bank Nifty straddles, a position with significant negative gamma, alongside a simple long Nifty futures position. The risk head currently uses delta-normal Parametric VaR for the entire book to keep the daily risk report fast to produce.
body.prompt: Where is this choice most likely to understate real risk, and what would you recommend instead?
body.modelAnswer: The short straddle position is the concern, not the futures position. Delta-normal VaR approximates the straddle's sharply curved, negative-gamma payoff with a straight line, which will understate how much the position can lose if Bank Nifty makes a large move in either direction, exactly the move that hurts a short-gamma position most. The futures position is linear, so Parametric VaR is a reasonable fit there. A sensible recommendation is to run Monte Carlo with full revaluation specifically for the options book, or the whole book if compute allows, while keeping Parametric VaR as a fast daily estimate for the linear positions, cross-checking the two periodically.

body.text: Monte Carlo does not remove the need to choose a distribution, it just lets you choose a better one, and lets you reprice anything, however nonlinear, exactly, instead of approximating it.

points: Monte Carlo VaR simulates thousands of possible future paths from a chosen model, fully revalues the portfolio on each, then sorts and reads off the percentile, the same last step as Historical Simulation.
Using normal draws, Monte Carlo VaR should converge close to the closed-form Parametric VaR figure, a useful sanity check on the simulation.
Fat-tailed draws, like Student-t, do not raise VaR uniformly across confidence levels, they can lower it slightly at 95% while raising it substantially at 99% or beyond.
Full revaluation at each simulated outcome is what lets Monte Carlo correctly price convex, nonlinear payoffs like options, fixing the delta-normal blind spot from the Parametric method.
Every Monte Carlo result carries simulation error tied to the number of paths run, and it still depends entirely on the distribution and correlation assumptions chosen going in.
